question: How does dynamic chunking determine or adapt sequence chunk boundaries?
answer:
Dynamic chunking determines and adapts chunk boundaries by learning them directly from the data during training, rather than fixing them a priori.  
In the H‑Net architecture, each chunking layer contains a **routing module** that examines the similarity between adjacent token‑level representations produced by the encoder.  The module computes cosine similarity between consecutive encoder outputs; when the similarity drops (i.e., the context shifts), the routing module assigns a higher probability that a boundary should be placed there.  These boundary probabilities are then turned into hard boundary indicators, which the **downsampler** uses to keep only the vectors at the chosen boundaries, thereby compressing low‑information regions while preserving high‑information content.  Because the routing module and the rest of the network are trained end‑to‑end, the learned boundaries adapt to the semantic structure of each input sequence.  

> *“H‑Net learns chunking boundaries through end‑to‑end training, allowing it to identify semantically meaningful units adaptively.”*  
> *“The routing module implements this intuition through cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs.”*  
> *“Given encoder outputs ˆX, it calculates boundary probabilities pt and boundary indicators bt.”*  

These mechanisms enable the dynamic chunking module to compress data to a resolution comparable to BPE tokenizers (≈4.5–5 bytes per chunk) and to discover meaningful boundaries without any external supervision

A.1.1 Isotropic Architectures

The most direct approach to modeling language with tokenizers is to simply model raw byte sequences with a standard
sequence model architecture. Since this naive approach suffers from computational challenges on long sequences, Mam-
baByte (Wang et al. 2024) proposed using a state space model for its linear-time efficiency. We similarly use Mamba(-2)
(Dao and Gu 2024) layers in the outer stages of an H-Net. Notably, through extensive ablations we show that Mamba is not
just more efficient but also better at modeling high-resolution data such as text characters and DNA base pairs.

A.1.2 Static Chunking

To reduce sequence length, several approaches downsample the input sequence hierarchically. The most straightforward
methods operate independently of input context, partitioning sequences using fixed-size intervals. Many strategies could
be used to aggregate a width-𝑘window, including direct downsampling, average pooling, linear transformations that mix
across the chunk, convolutions, and more; we lump these together as pooling operations.

2.2 Dynamic Chunking (DC)

H-Net learns chunking boundaries through end-to-end training, allowing it to identify semantically meaningful units
adaptively. Furthermore, this dynamic approach enables the model to allocate computational resources efficiently by
compressing low-information regions while preserving high-information content at appropriate granularity.

These limitations stem from the static nature of predefined vocabularies, which cannot adapt their chunking strategies to

To address these constraints, tokenizer-free methods have emerged that avoid the reliance on predefined vocabularies.
